newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive - MMP mating dances.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive - MMP mating dances.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Sept 3 - Political parties, already deep into electioneering though some have yet to launch their campaigns officially, are being exceptionally coy about their prospective partners in the mating dance that will follow the country's first mixed-member proportional election.

New Zealand First will not do a deal with National while Jim Bolger is its leader; Labour will not join any other party unless it is the senior partner in a coalition; the Alliance has refused, in advance, to enter a coalition because it says a coalition agreement must be spelt out before the election.
ACT, meanwhile, insists it should not be looked on as a "junior" National Party.
It's baffling for the average voter, still getting to grips with the new voting system that carries two votes, one for a party and one for an electorate MP.

Former Prime Minister David Lange, using his valedictory speech in parliament to urge a reconciliation between the Alliance and Labour (spurned immediately by Alliance leader Jim Anderton) laments that there is a lack of cohesion on the left in New Zealand politics.

The Alliance, he says, has in effect decided not to play a serious part in politics: Anderton is the only leader entering the election on a commitment that neither he nor his party will form part of a government.
Lange predicts that the election will return Jim Bolger as the leader with the largest single block in the new parliament. "He's not going to win a majority, so he'll have to cast about him."
National's prospects have taken a dip according to the latest opinion poll by the Colmar Brunton group.

Where for most of the year its support has been tracking in the mid-forties, now it is down to 35 percent, which would give it only 47 seats, well short of the 60-plus a party needs to govern on its own.

But as National has slipped in the polls, prospective coalition partners in the shape of ACT and the Christian Coalition have risen -- though both are only hovering around the five percent mark. (Under the MMP system New Zealand has chosen, a party needs to cross the five percent threshold to be assured of seats in parliament).
With 60 percent of voters displaying antipathy towards National, political pundits have argued that a coalition of left-leaning parties would be the most likely outcome of the election.
And for most of the year Labour has been treating NZ First with kid gloves, in the expectation that the two could work together after the election.

It has been reinforced in that belief by the conciliatory attitude in particular of NZ First's deputy leader Tau Henare, who has made it clear that he has more sympathy for Labour on social policy than for National.

But illusions were shattered last week when NZ First leaders Winston Peters unleashed a vitriolic attack on Labour, accusing it of being the "ultimate political quisling" for its complicity with the government in the sale of Forestcorp to a consortium that included, along with two big companies, a Chinese government controlled corporation.

Whether Peters was worried by his own slippage in opinion polls, or whether he believes that Labour is in terminal decline, his onslaught has left Labour MPs pondering about the reliability of NZ First as an ally.
Peters may also see an opportunity, by attacking Labour, to hoover up support by erstwhile National voters in rural New Zealand.

For, virtually in the same breath, he has hit out at Federated Farmers for backing economic policies which he says are crippling the country's major farm export industries. Federated Farmers has "bought" the Treasury line and its leadership is trapped in a time warp, according to Peters.
Peters detects disenchantment in provincial New Zealand for both Labour and National, and is going out after a block of voters big enough, he believes, to put him "over the top".
In any case, his performance has reinforced the advice of a visiting Israeli political pundit Zeev Segal, who on the outcome of that mating dance warns "never say never".
It's dangerous, says Professor Segal, to assume that apparently entrenched positions of political parties before the election rule out anything that might happen after it.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
